24-097.r: Not correct: 'Money Bill introduced in Rajya Sabha' → only in Lok Sabha (Art 109(1)); Rajya Sabha returns it, with or without recommendations, within 14 days.

24-103.r: Rajya Sabha can delay a Money Bill (treated here as 'Finance Bill') for at most fourteen days; an ordinary bill has no time limit.

24-105.r: Money Bill amended by Rajya Sabha → deemed passed once Lok Sabha passes it again, accepting or rejecting the changes (Art 109); no joint session, no special majority.

24-106.r: Bill merely involving expenditure from Consolidated Fund (Financial Bill, Art 117(3)) → can be introduced in either House; President's recommendation needed for its consideration.
24-106.t: Financial Bill under Art 117(1) (Art 110 matters) is Lok Sabha-only; 117(3) expenditure bill can start in either House.

24-107.r: Annual Financial Statement (Union Budget) → Article 112; financial year 1 April to 31 March; budget passes through six stages in Parliament.

24-108.r: Art 112 → President causes the Annual Financial Statement (Budget), estimated receipts and expenditure, to be laid before both Houses each financial year.

24-109.r: 'Budget' does not appear in the Constitution; it uses 'Annual Financial Statement' (Art 112); Appropriation Bill and Consolidated Fund of India do appear.

24-110.r: Not correct: 'Parliament votes on charged expenditure' → charged expenditure on Consolidated Fund (Art 112(3)) is only discussed, never voted.

24-111.r: Parliamentary control over finance: Annual Financial Statement, Appropriation Bill before withdrawal (Art 114), supplementary grants and vote on account (Arts 115, 116), Finance Bill; no Budget Office review.

24-112.r: If Lok Sabha does not pass the Union Budget → PM submits resignation of the Council of Ministers (government has lost its majority).

24-113.r: Private member's Bill → by any MP other than a Minister (not only nominated MPs); about a dozen passed since independence, so not a recent first.

24-114.r: Economic Survey → presented in Parliament every year before the Budget; reviews progress and fiscal details of economic sectors for the current year.

24-115.r: Vote on Account (Art 116) → lets Union Government withdraw money from Consolidated Fund for a specific period when Appropriation Bill is not yet passed.

24-116.r: Vote on Account (Art 116(1)(a)) → funds to run the administration pending passage of the full budget, e.g. near elections or before new financial year.

24-118.r: Vote on Account covers only expenditure; Interim Budget covers both receipts and expenditure; the 'stable vs caretaker government' distinction is false.
24-118.t: Don't treat Vote on Account and Interim Budget as same: only Interim Budget shows receipts.

24-119.r: Estimates of expenditure → submitted to Lok Sabha as Demands for Grants (Art 113(2)); Lok Sabha may assent, refuse or reduce them.

24-120.r: Normal financial legislation: Budget presentation → discussion → Appropriation Bill → Finance Bill; Vote on Account, vote of credit, exceptional grants (Art 116) are outside it.

24-121.r: President's prior sanction needed before Bills on: forming a new State, altering State boundaries, taxation in which States are interested, and Money Bills.

24-122.r: Censure Motion differs from No-Confidence Motion: reasons must be stated; no separate leave of the House needed.
24-122.c: Book prints two answers, (b) and (d); BPSC deleted the question.

24-123.r: Cut motion → linked to Union Budget (opposes/reduces a demand for grant); types: token, policy, frugality cut; Censure, Calling Attention, Adjournment are non-budget motions.

24-124.r: Cut motion → proposal to reduce a demand for grant in the budget; types: Disapproval of Policy, Economy and Token cut.

24-125.r: Cut Motion → motion to reduce the amount of a demand for grants; aims to draw the House's attention to the matter specified.

24-126.r: Wrong pair: Vote on Account (Art 116) only draws money till budget passes, not yearly sanction; Policy cut → Re one; Economy cut → set amount; Token cut → Rs one hundred.

24-127.r: Calling Attention (Indian innovation) → draws a Minister's attention to an urgent public matter; it has restricted the scope of the Adjournment Motion (no censure element).

24-128.r: Parliament controls Council of Ministers through Adjournment Motion, Question Hour and Supplementary Questions; starred → oral with supplementaries; unstarred → no supplementaries.

24-129.r: Starred question (marked *) → oral answer, supplementaries allowed, max 20 listed a day; unstarred → not answered orally, no supplementaries.

24-130.r: Adjournment motion → allows discussion on a definite matter of urgent public importance.

24-131.r: Rule 184 (Lok Sabha) → discussion followed by voting; government avoids it as a lost vote can threaten it. A and R true, R explains A.

24-132.r: Rule 377 → matters not raisable under other rules; notice to Secretary-General; Speaker's consent needed; daily limit raised from 20 to 30 in 2015.
24-132.c: Answer not printed; current limit (30) matches no option; the older limit was 20.

24-133.r: Guillotine → a closure motion: undiscussed clauses are put to vote with discussed ones when time is over, cutting short debate on the bill.

24-134.r: President can issue ordinance (Art 123) except when both Houses are in session; NDC is presided by the PM, so 'FM + CMs' is wrong.

24-135.r: Right to Property → legal right (Art 300-A) by 44th Amendment, 1978; Rajya Sabha can hold a non-Money Finance Bill; 42nd Amendment, 1976 added Socialist and Secular, not Democratic.

24-136.r: Each House of Parliament has a separate secretariat independent of the Government (Art 98); idea mooted in January 1926 by Vithalbhai J. Patel.

24-137.r: Art 98(1): separate secretariat staff for each House, but common posts allowed; Art 98(2): Parliament may by law regulate their recruitment and service conditions.

24-138.r: Sovereignty of Indian Parliament → restricted by judicial review; its laws cannot violate the Basic Structure of the Constitution.

24-139.r: Golden Jubilee of Indian Parliament → 13 May 2002 (Parliament constituted 13 May 1952), marking 50 years.

24-140.r: New Parliament building → designed by Bimal Patel; inaugurated by PM Narendra Modi on 28 May 2023; old building by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker.

24-141.r: Indian Parliamentary Group → autonomous body (1949, motion of 16 August 1948); open to MPs and ex-MPs; Lok Sabha Speaker is ex-officio President; IPU national group.
24-141.c: Answer not printed; explanation finds (ii) and (iii) true, a combination no option offers.

24-142.r: Nationalist elected Speaker of Central Legislative Assembly in 1925 → Vithalbhai Patel, first to hold it (24 August 1925 to 28 April 1930).

25-001.r: Parliament controls the administration through Parliamentary Committees (Public Accounts, Estimates, Standing Committees).

25-002.r: Financial Committees of Parliament → Public Accounts Committee, Estimates Committee and Committee on Public Undertakings.
25-002.h: Financial trio 'PEP': Public Accounts, Estimates, Public Undertakings.

25-003.r: Largest Parliamentary Committee → Estimates Committee (30 members, all Lok Sabha, first 1950, one-year term); PAC 22 (15 + 7); Public Undertakings 22; Petitions 15.

25-006.r: Not a Parliamentary tool → CAG (independent constitutional authority, Art 148); PAC, Estimates Committee and Public Undertakings Committee are Parliament's tools.

25-007.r: Parliament's joint Standing Committees → Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha members roughly in ratio 2:1.

25-008.r: PAC Chairman → appointed by Lok Sabha Speaker; PAC = 22 MPs (15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha), no outside experts; assisted by CAG.

25-009.r: Public Accounts Committee → formed every year, not more than 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha, 7 from Rajya Sabha; scrutinises the CAG's report.

25-011.r: PAC → examines CAG's annual audit reports; financial check on the executive; first set up 1921 under Government of India Act, 1919; 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS).

25-012.r: Estimates Committee (30) all from Lok Sabha; PAC and Public Undertakings (22 = 15 LS + 7 RS); Parliamentary Affairs Ministry under Cabinet Committee; its Minister nominates MPs to government bodies.

25-013.r: PAC's main function → examine Government's accounts and CAG's report on Union accounts; exposes misuse of public expenditure.
